mstts:express-as.prosody: Let’s talk about Chapter 7: Education—The Double-Edged Sword. Think back to your earliest memories of school. For a lot of us, that classroom is the first place where we’re introduced to the “official” version of history. Maybe you remember feeling proud as you learned about heroes and great achievements. Or maybe, you felt a little lost—searching those pages for a story that sounded like your own, but coming up empty. The classroom isn’t just a place to memorize dates and facts. It’s where our sense of identity can start to take shape—or sometimes, where it gets challenged. Picture this: a teacher stands at the front, reading from a textbook that’s seen better days. Some students hang on every word, curious and eager. Others? They’re skeptical, maybe even bored. Then, one brave kid raises a hand, asking about a historical figure from their own neighborhood or culture. The teacher pauses, searching for an answer that isn’t in the book. The moment slips by, but that question—why isn’t my story here?—lingers long after. It’s a powerful reminder that education can do two things at once. On one hand, it opens doors. It sparks curiosity, encourages us to think critically, to explore new ideas. But on the other hand, it can shut doors, too. It can reinforce narrow views, silence voices that don’t fit the standard narrative, and even deepen the gaps between us. The stories we hear—or don’t hear—in school send strong signals about whose lives really matter. Now, there are schools and teachers out there trying to change this. They’re expanding the curriculum, bringing in voices that have been ignored for far too long. Maybe they invite guest speakers, introduce new books, or ask students to research their own family histories. And when that happens? You can feel the difference. Students who once felt invisible start to see themselves in the stories they study. They grow more confident, feel a real sense of belonging, and start seeing the world with new eyes. But let’s be honest—change isn’t always easy. Not everyone welcomes new stories. Some worry that including different perspectives will shake up old beliefs. Debates break out about what should be taught, and how. It gets messy. Sometimes it’s uncomfortable. But it’s also essential. For education to truly deliver on its promise, it has to face the past honestly, and be open to all the messy, beautiful complexity of human experience.
